sections.body:
Ordering food in a foreign country looks like a language test, and it is not. It is a small transaction with a fixed order of parts, and the parts are the same in every country. Learn the order and you can eat anywhere.

A meal has four actors. **You** are the customer. The **waiter** or **waitress** takes the order and brings the food. The **cook** makes it. The **owner** sets the prices and the rules. In a small place these people are the same two or three individuals, and in a large restaurant they are not.

The order itself usually runs like this: you are seated, you are given a menu, you may be asked for drinks first, you order, the food comes, you ask for the bill, you pay, you may leave a tip. Between those points there is only one real difficulty, which is the menu itself.

The menu is a price list with short descriptions. Behind every line there are facts you cannot see: how much food it is, how it is cooked, what is in it, and how hot it will be. The words on the menu are usually the easiest part, because the vocabulary of cooking is small. There are about forty common words, and the same words appear on every menu in every language.

Two habits make this much easier. First, point at the item as well as saying it, because pointing is a universal language. Second, never be afraid to ask one question: "What is this?", "Is it spicy?", "How much is it?" A restaurant expects these questions. A traveller who asks one clear question in a strange language gets a better answer than a traveller who orders in silence and regrets it.

Behind the counter is a **kitchen** with its own grammar. An order goes in as a ticket, and a ticket has a time. That is why a simple dish can take thirty minutes in a busy restaurant while a complicated one is on the table in ten: the kitchen cooks many things at once, and it works on timing, not on sequence. It is also why the thing you did not order may arrive first, and why the missing dish may turn up unannounced after you have eaten everything else.

Two consequences follow for you. Order early if you have a flight or a show to make, because the kitchen has no idea what time your train leaves. And if you are in a hurry, eat at the counter, where the food is often turned faster than in the dining room.
examples: Could you tell me what this dish is?
Is this one spicy, please?
sections.heading: What ordering food actually involves

sections.body:
You do not need to know the language to read a menu. You need to know what to look for, and menus follow a layout almost everywhere.

Look at the shape first. Drinks are usually at the top or the side, listed with prices per glass or per bottle. Starters come before main courses, and desserts come at the end. A section headed by a price range, a set price, or a word meaning "menu of the day" is usually a good, fixed-price choice for a first meal.

The price tells you the scale. A main course that costs a small amount is small, and one that costs a large amount is generous. You cannot know the local currency, so compare prices within the menu: if the most expensive main course is four times the cheapest, you have a range. The price is also a hint about the restaurant: the same dish in a different street can be double.

Numbers are often your anchor. Even in a language you cannot read, you can recognise numbers, and many menus print the weight or the size. A dish marked 250 g is not a dish marked 800 g, and in many countries the price is per weight for some dishes, especially in markets and street kitchens.

Watch the cooking words. Words like grilled, fried, steamed, raw, boiled, roasted, baked, smoked and stewed appear in every language and are usually cognates or near-cognates of the English word. They also warn you: grilled and fried are brown and crisp, steamed and boiled are soft and plain, and raw is raw.

Look at the pictures, but treat them as decoration. Photos show a typical plate, not your plate. The dish in the picture is often larger and better arranged than the one that arrives, and it may contain ingredients that were left out of the dish you ordered.

And notice the one thing every menu can tell you even in a language you cannot read: the **allergens**. A short list of symbols or letters, often the same across the country, marks dishes with nuts, dairy, gluten, eggs, shellfish or soy. Look for that block first, and it protects you.
examples: Is this price for the whole dish or for 100 grams?
Could you show me the picture of the soup?
Which of these has no nuts in it?
sections.heading: How to read a menu you cannot read

sections.body:
A menu has a small vocabulary and it repeats. These are the words you will meet on almost every menu in Europe, Asia and the Americas.

A **starter** or **appetiser** comes first and is usually small: soup, salad, fried snacks, a slice of bread with something on it. A **main course** is the big dish. **Sides** come with it and are usually shared. A **dessert** is sweet and comes last. A **set menu** or **fixed menu** is a starter, a main and a dessert sold together at one price, and it is usually the best value and the safest choice in a country you do not know.

Soup is soup, **salad** is salad, **steak** is steak, and **fish**, **chicken**, **beef**, **pork** and **lamb** are the same in most menus, often with the local spelling rather than the English one. **Rice**, **noodles**, **bread** and **chips** appear constantly.

Two words describe the cooking and the risk. **Spicy** or **hot** means chilli, and the strength varies enormously. **Raw** or **undercooked** is a warning you should take seriously, particularly with meat, fish and eggs.

And the drink vocabulary: **still water** is still, **sparkling water** is fizzy, **tap water** is from the tap, and **bottled water** is sealed. **House wine** is the cheapest wine the house sells, by the glass or the jug. **Draft** or ** draught** beer is from the tap, and a **bottle** is what it sounds like. **Aperitif** is a drink before the meal, and it is often cheaper than the same wine later.
examples: I will have the set menu with a starter of soup.
Is the fish grilled or fried?
I would like still water, please.
sections.heading: The words a menu is built from

terms.example: Could we see the menu, please?
terms.gloss: The list of dishes a kitchen offers, with prices and short descriptions.

terms.example: I will take the set menu, please.
terms.gloss: A starter, a main course and a dessert sold together at a single price. Often the cheapest and most predictable choice.

terms.example: As a starter, I will have the soup.
terms.gloss: The small first course, such as soup, a salad or fried snacks.

terms.example: What would you recommend for the main course?
terms.gloss: The main dish of the meal, usually the largest and most expensive item.

terms.example: Do you have any sugar-free desserts?
terms.gloss: The sweet course at the end of the meal, or the sweet things served with coffee.

sections.body:
This is the part of the meal where a mistake can be serious, and where a few English sentences are worth learning by heart.

An **allergy** is not the same as a dislike. Tell the waiter clearly: "I have a nut allergy. Is this dish safe?" Say **allergy**, not "I do not like nuts", because the second sentence is understood as a preference and the first triggers a check. In a serious case, ask them to check with the kitchen, and if the restaurant is busy or the dish is complex, choose something simpler where the ingredients are obvious.

A **dietary restriction** is a rule you follow, often religious: halal, kosher, vegetarian, vegan. The words are widely used in menus and in restaurants in most countries, and the symbols for them are usually printed on the menu. Say it early: "Is this halal?" or "Is there any pork in this?" Some countries have a standard halal mark on the certificate displayed in the window; some restaurants are certified, some only say they cook to the rule, and those are not the same.

A **vegetarian** dish contains no meat or fish, and it may still contain eggs, dairy and honey. A **vegan** dish contains no animal products at all, and it is harder to find than vegetarian food. A dish marked **vegetarian** in a country where vegetarian cooking is the norm may still be cooked in animal fat, so it matters where you are.

Other things worth asking about: whether the food is **spicy**, whether it contains **pork**, whether a dish is **halal**, and whether a soup is made with **pork broth**. One more useful habit: ask whether the **kitchen handles nuts or shellfish**, because in a busy kitchen the same fryer and the same board are used for many dishes.
examples: I have a nut allergy. Is this dish safe?
Is there any pork in this soup?
Is this suitable for vegetarians?
sections.heading: Allergies, religious rules and preferences

terms.example: I have a shellfish allergy. Is this dish safe for me?
terms.gloss: A medical reaction to a food, which can be dangerous. It must be told to the staff as an allergy, not as a dislike.

terms.example: Do you have any halal dishes that do not contain pork?
terms.gloss: A rule you follow about what you eat, often religious or ethical, such as halal, kosher, vegetarian or vegan.

sections.body:
The mechanics of a meal are the same everywhere, and knowing them removes the last bit of stress. The sequence below is normal in a restaurant; in a café or a street stall you simply skip the parts that do not exist.

Sit where you are shown. Staff seat you; do not choose a table first unless the place is empty and you are sure it is free. In some countries the host takes your booking for a table, and in some the waiter carries the menu.

Get a drink first. Usually water, and often still water unless you ask for sparkling. This is the moment to ask the one practical question: "Is the service charge included?" or "What is the set menu?"

Order in the order of the meal. Drinks, then a starter, then the main course, then sides if you need them, then dessert. If you are unsure, order the first course and the main and add the rest after. You can always order more later; you cannot easily undo a dish that is already cooking.

Use the simplest safe order when the language is hard. "The set menu, please" is a complete sentence in every language, and it is the single most useful phrase a traveller can learn.

Say what you do not want, and ask about the hot thing. "Not spicy, please" is understood everywhere, and "medium spicy" or "a little spicy" keeps you in control.

Check before the plates arrive. If you ordered without dairy and the dish has cream on it, say so immediately. Once it is on the table, it is much harder.

Ask for the bill when you are ready, and use the local phrase for it if you know it. In much of Asia the bill is brought with the receipt, in much of Europe the waiter brings it when you ask, and in North America you ask at the desk. A confident "the bill, please" is understood in every case.
examples: The set menu, please.
Not spicy, or only a little spicy.
Could we have the bill, please?
sections.heading: Ordering, from the door to the table
steps: Follow the staff to a table and wait to be greeted.
Order water and ask what the set menu includes.
Order a starter and a main course, or the set menu.
Say clearly: not spicy, or how spicy.
Check the dish before you start eating it.
Ask for the bill when you have finished.

sections.body:
Paying abroad has two surprises for newcomers, and both are legitimate customs rather than traps.

The first is the **service charge**. In many countries a percentage, usually 10 % or 15 %, is added to the bill automatically and is often shown as a separate line called "service" or "service compris". When it is included, you do not tip on top of it, because you would be paying for the same service twice. When it is not included, and the staff are paid by the hour, a tip is expected. The restaurant usually states the rule on the menu or on a small card at the table, and if you cannot find it, ask the waiter: "Is service included?" That one question removes all doubt.

The second is the **tip**. The custom differs sharply by country. In the United States a tip of 18 % to 20 % is normal and is often added automatically, with extra for good service. In much of Europe the service charge covers it, and a small rounding or a few coins is enough. In Japan and Korea, tipping is not part of the culture and can cause confusion, because the service charge already covers it. In much of Southeast Asia and the Middle East, a small tip of 5 % to 10 % is appreciated. In Vietnam, many restaurants add a service charge for groups, and rounding up or leaving a small amount is friendly.

The practical rule: look at the bill for a service line, then look at the menu for the local custom, and when in doubt ask. "Is a tip expected?" is a question no waiter anywhere finds offensive.

How to pay. Cards are accepted in most cities, but not everywhere: smaller restaurants, market stalls and street kitchens are often cash only, and in some countries a card payment adds a surcharge. Ask before you order: "Can I pay by card?" Cash in small notes is the safest option. Keep the receipt until you have left, because a disputed bill is very hard to argue without it.

And **never leave your card on the table**. Pay at the desk, or ask the waiter to bring the machine to you.
examples: Is service included, or should I leave a tip?
Can I pay by card, or do you take cash only?
Could I have the receipt, please?
sections.heading: The bill, the service charge and the tip

terms.example: Could we have the bill, please? Is service included?
terms.gloss: The list of what you ordered and what you owe. In America it is called the check.

terms.example: The service charge is already on the bill, so we will just round it up.
terms.gloss: A percentage added to the bill for service, usually 10 % or 15 %. When it is included, tipping again is not expected.

terms.example: Is a tip expected, or is service included?
terms.gloss: A small extra payment for good service. The amount and the custom differ in every country, so check before you pay.

sections.body:
Restaurants use a small set of marks on menus, and they are worth recognising before you order rather than after.

The letter **V** in many European menus means **vegetarian**. It is a quick, cheap sign, and in some countries it is legally protected, so it means something. A **vegan** dish is usually marked with the word itself, or with a V and a small extra mark, and it is always worth confirming, because in some languages the word for vegan also means "not a vegetarian".

Halal is usually written in Arabic or marked with the Arabic word, sometimes with a certificate logo in the window. **Kosher** is marked with a K, a star or a Hebrew letter. A **gluten-free** mark is increasingly common in Europe and Australia.

Some menus use **pepper symbols** to show heat: one chilli for mild, three for very hot, and often a **chilli with a cross** for a dish with no chilli at all. And some menus use an **asterisk or a footnote** for a dish that contains an allergen, with a key at the bottom of the page. That key is the most important small print on the whole menu.

Two practical notes. Symbols are often printed in the local language only, so a traveller with no language at all should look at the allergen key and ask. And in countries where the symbols are legally controlled, a restaurant that marks a dish correctly is reliable; in countries where they are not, treat them as a hint and still ask.
examples: What does the V mean on this menu?
Is the starred dish safe for people with nuts?
How hot is this, on a scale of one to three?
sections.heading: The symbols that mark a dish

symbols.meaning: The letter V: the dish contains no meat or fish. It may still contain eggs, dairy or honey.
The word halal, or Arabic script: the dish is prepared according to Islamic rules.
A K, a star or a Hebrew letter: the dish is certified kosher.
One, two or three chillies: how hot the dish is.
An asterisk with a key at the foot of the menu: the dish contains one of the listed allergens.

sections.body:
Ordering the wrong thing. Point at the dish as well as naming it, and confirm before the order is written down. "This one, here" plus the name removes almost every mistake.

Ignoring the heat. "Spicy" in one country can mean gentle. Say "not spicy" clearly, and if the first bite is too hot, say so: "It is too spicy for me", and ask for the dish without chilli. Most kitchens will oblige.

Accepting a dish and eating it anyway. If it is not what you ordered, say so while it is still on the table. After you have eaten half of it, the kitchen will argue that the dish was fine.

Drinking the tap water in a place where you should not. In most countries the tap water is safe, but in some it is not. If you are unsure, order bottled or filtered water. Ice is a separate question: in a hot country, ice from a machine is usually fine, ice from a bucket in the street is usually not.

Paying in the wrong currency or at the wrong exchange rate. When a tourist menu lists prices in both currencies, the local currency is the real one. And if you change money at an airport or a hotel counter, the rate is usually worse than a bank or an ATM.

Getting sick after a meal. If something tastes wrong, do not force it down to be polite. Send it back, and if you feel unwell, keep the receipt and ask the staff for help, and contact your insurer if you have one.
sections.heading: How meals go wrong, and how to stop them

sections.body:
Three things can go wrong at the end of a meal: the dish arrives wrong, the food makes you ill, or the bill is wrong. Each has a simple procedure.

The wrong dish arrives. Say it at once, calmly, and use the name of your dish: "I ordered the grilled fish, but this is the fried one." Most errors are a mix-up in the kitchen, and kitchens fix them. Be polite and specific, and do not accuse anybody. If the kitchen cannot fix it, ask for something else at the same price, or for the dish to be removed from the bill.

The food makes you ill. Stop eating. Tell the staff immediately, in plain words: "I feel sick after eating this." Ask them to keep the plate. If the reaction is severe, do not wait: ask for the address of the nearest clinic and contact your travel insurance. Keeping the receipt and the plate makes a claim possible.

The bill looks wrong. Read it item by item against what you ordered and what was on the table. Look for the difference between what you ordered and what was charged, and for a service charge you did not expect. Then ask the waiter, in a low voice, at the table: "Can you explain this line, please?" Most errors are genuine mistakes, and they are corrected at the table. If the answer is unsatisfactory, ask for the manager, and pay the part you do not dispute, keeping the rest.

Throughout all three, remember the cultural setting. In most countries a complaint handled politely, at the table, is taken seriously and is not seen as rude. Rude, loud and public is what turns a solvable problem into a scene.

And one last piece of advice: if the meal goes badly, eat something else. A cheap alternative near the station is always better than a night in an unfamiliar bathroom.
examples: I ordered the grilled fish, but this one is fried. Could you change it?
I feel sick after eating this. Could we keep the plate?
Could you explain this line on the bill, please?
sections.heading: When the meal is wrong

terms.example: Let us get something from a street stall near the station instead of waiting for a table.
terms.gloss: Food bought from a stall or a small kitchen at the roadside. It is usually cheap, quick and freshly cooked, but the hygiene is worth watching.

item.summary: A menu in a language you do not read is a short problem with a known solution. After reading this you can read any menu, order exactly what you want, explain a dietary need, pay the right amount and tip in the local way.
item.title: Ordering Food in a Foreign Country
